title: Services and Dependency Injection
summary: Move shared state and logic into services, provide them once for the whole app with providedIn root, obtain them with inject(), and know when a component-level provider is the better choice.
introduction: Two components that need the same data, a cart badge in the header and a product page, cannot share it through inputs: they are too far apart in the tree. The Angular answer is a service, a plain class that holds state and logic, handed to any component that asks for it by the dependency injection system. This lesson builds a cart service with signals, uses it from two components, configures values with injection tokens and explains the rules about where inject() may be called.
learningObjectives: Create a singleton service with providedIn root and signals
Obtain services and configuration values with inject() and InjectionToken
Decide between root-level and component-level providers

blocks.text: Components should be about presentation. Business rules (what is in the cart, whether the user is logged in, how to talk to the API) belong in classes that have no template and can be tested without a DOM. **Dependency injection** (DI) is how components get hold of those classes: instead of creating them with `new`, a component asks Angular for an instance, and Angular decides whether to create a new one or hand over the one it already has. That makes sharing state trivial and swapping implementations in tests a one-liner.

`@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })` registers the class with the application-wide injector. Angular creates **one** instance the first time something asks for it and reuses it everywhere after that. Keep the writable signal private and expose a read-only view plus methods that change it, so every write goes through the service.

blocks.title: src/app/cart-service.ts

blocks.text: `ng generate service cart` creates this file skeleton (named `cart.ts` with the class `Cart` under the Angular 20 naming style, or `cart-service.ts` with `CartService` if you prefer the explicit suffix; both are fine, as long as a project is consistent).
`inject(CartService)` in a field initialiser asks the injector for the instance. Two unrelated components get the same object, so a change made through one is immediately visible in the other.

blocks.text: The badge never talks to the product component. It reads the service's `count` and `total` signals in its template, so Angular re-renders it whenever the cart changes. `protected` makes the field visible to the template while keeping it out of the public API of the class; `private` fields cannot be used in templates.

blocks.title: Common mistake: calling inject() in the wrong place
blocks.text: `inject()` only works in an **injection context**: a constructor, a field initialiser, a provider factory, or a function wrapped in `runInInjectionContext`. Calling it inside a method or an event handler throws `NG0203: inject() must be called from an injection context such as a constructor, a factory function, a field initializer, or a function used with runInInjectionContext`. Inject what you need into a field at construction time and use the field later.

Older code injects through constructor parameters: `constructor(private cart: CartService) {}`. It still works, but `inject()` is shorter, works in functions such as route guards, and does not break when a class is extended. New Angular 22 code uses `inject()`.

DI is not only for classes. An `InjectionToken` names a value, such as an API base URL, that is provided in `app.config.ts` and injected wherever needed. Tests or a second environment can provide a different value without touching the code that uses it.

blocks.title: src/app/api-url.ts, src/app/app.config.ts and a service

blocks.text: Asking for something that was never provided throws `NG0201: No provider for API_URL!`. Pass `{ optional: true }` as the second argument of `inject()` when a missing value is acceptable; you then get `null` instead of an error.

Injectors form a tree that mirrors the component tree. When a component calls `inject()`, Angular looks in the component's own injector, then its parent's, and so on up to the root. Adding a class to a component's `providers` array creates a **separate instance for each instance of that component**, shared with its children but invisible to the rest of the app.

blocks.title: Testing is where DI pays off
blocks.text: In a test, `TestBed.configureTestingModule({ providers: [{ provide: CartService, useValue: fakeCart }] })` replaces the real service for every component under test. The [testing lesson](/tutorials/angular/testing) uses this to test a component without a backend.

questions.question: Where may `inject(CartService)` be called?
questions.explanation: Field initialisers and constructors run inside an injection context. Methods and event handlers run later, when no injection context is active.
options: In a field initialiser or the constructor
In any method of the class

questions.question: Adding a service to a component's `providers` array gives every instance of that component its own copy of the service.
questions.explanation: Component-level providers create one instance per component instance, shared only with that component's descendants.

seo.title: Angular Services and Dependency Injection with inject()
seo.description: Learn Angular 22 services: providedIn root singletons with signals, the inject() function, InjectionToken for configuration, and component-level providers.
